source.title: Tied Crosscoders: Explaining Chat Behavior from Base Model

record.tranche_reason: The study discusses polysemanticity and analyzes SAE/crosscoder latents, but it does not test superposition, feature competition for network dimensions, or any of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported experiments concern model-diffing, latent-set overlap, and similarity between crosscoder latents. These are adjacent findings, not tests of the claimed superposition geometry or its capacity account. The SAE results do not establish that dictionary features are complete or canonical, and the text gives no feature-versus-dimension geometry results.
record.test_reason: The post uses SAEs and crosscoders as tools for model-diffing between Gemma 2 base and chat models. Its results concern its own tied-crosscoder method and feature-correlation changes from fine-tuning. It reports no test of superposition geometry, capacity-driven polysemanticity, or SAE completeness or canonicity. T4 fits better than T6, because the work depends on dictionary features as units.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly right. The authors add that fine-tuning appears to enhance existing base-model mechanisms, which the chat model reuses in new contexts. They also claim the tied crosscoder gives a quantitative measure of latent novelty, and they frame the post as a research update.
record.recipe_differences: The study presents a tied crosscoder for model-diffing; it does not reproduce or test the original superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The author says only eta=2 was tried and suggests that a smaller eta might yield more interpretable results.

fits_no_version.finding: In a standard crosscoder, one concept (e.g. blue/green after correlation-altering fine-tuning) can appear as two model-exclusive latents with decoder cosine similarity 0.97. Exclusive latents are more similar to other latents than shared latents are.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary latents in crosscoders depend on architecture and loss. A single concept can be split into duplicate exclusive latents.

fits_no_version.finding: The Jaccard overlap of Cannot and Harmful SAE latent sets is about 0.19 in Gemma-2-9b and about 0.39 in Gemma-2-9b-it. The authors call this a simple, preliminary experiment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Chat fine-tuning may increase correlation between refusal and harmfulness features.

record.problems: The text calls the feature-correlation experiment simple and acknowledges that another phenomenon could explain its result. Several conclusions are qualitative, and the author notes that further robust comparisons and tests remain to be done.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were included because the remaining examples and figures describe latent activations or interpretations without measuring the superposition claim or a listed version.

untested.parts: No toy-model superposition, sparsity transition or geometry is examined.
No test of whether neuron polysemanticity comes from capacity competition.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
SAEs and crosscoders are used, but whether features spread across neurons or are recoverable by a dictionary is not tested.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features in a single model are not tested. The crosscoder duplicate-latent finding concerns crosscoder design.
Whether features are one-dimensional or multi-dimensional is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: Some results are omitted but bear on no version: a 0.91 cosine shared latent in the half-swap vs base crosscoder, and the ratio plots in Figure 2. The post's summary numbers the experiments differently from its section headings. The rows follow the section headings.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test superposition, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry.
It does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by limited capacity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
It does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence for superposition.
The study uses SAE and crosscoder latents in LLMs, but does not test whether real-model features are distributed across neurons or whether a dictionary recovers the model's features.
The study does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
The study does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: Tied crosscoder on Gemma 2 2b and Gemma 2 2b it, compared with the standard crosscoder
rows.operation_detail: Qualitative comparison of base/chat latent monosemanticity

conditions.value: 250M tokens on a mixed dataset of the pile and LMSys chat data

rows.measure: Qualitative monosemanticity of base and chat latents
rows.baseline: Model-exclusive latents in the standard crosscoder
rows.value: The authors report that base and chat latents are considerably more monosemantic than model-exclusive latents in the standard crosscoder.
rows.note: A qualitative result about crosscoder latents; it does not measure capacity pressure or the dimensional geometry in the claim.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method (tied crosscoder) with the standard crosscoder by qualitative inspection. It is a method-performance comparison, not a result on the claim, and arguably should not be a row.

rows.subject: Standard crosscoder on Gemma-2-2b-no-swap and Gemma-2-2b-half-swap
rows.operation_detail: Compared decoder vectors for model-exclusive latents

conditions.value: 40k entries from each dataset, repeated to train up to 60M tokens

rows.measure: Cosine similarity between the no-swap and half-swap exclusive-latent decoder vectors
rows.note: The paper also states that each exclusive latent's top three positive logits contain blue and green. This concerns crosscoder behavior under an induced correlation manipulation, not the claim's superposition geometry.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b
rows.operation_detail: Compared sets of SAE latents selected by activation on Cannot versus Can prompts and Harmful versus Harmless prompts

conditions.value: 84 Cannot and 84 Can; 250 harmful and 250 harmless prompts

rows.measure: Jaccard overlap of the Cannot and Harmful latent sets
rows.baseline: Comparison with Gemma-2-9b-it, which has a reported overlap of approximately 0.39
rows.note: The authors describe this as a simple experiment and say another phenomenon could explain the result.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b-it
rows.operation_detail: Compared sets of SAE latents selected by activation on Cannot versus Can prompts and Harmful versus Harmless prompts

conditions.value: 84 Cannot and 84 Can; 250 harmful and 250 harmless prompts

rows.measure: Jaccard overlap of the Cannot and Harmful latent sets
rows.note: The authors interpret this as potential evidence that Cannot and Harmful features are more correlated in the chat model; it is not a test of superposition or SAE feature completeness.

rows.subject: Standard crosscoder on Gemma 2 2b and Gemma 2 2b it
rows.operation_detail: Compared maximum decoder-vector cosine similarity for exclusive latents against that for shared latents

conditions.value: relative decoder norm below 0.3 for base-exclusive and above 0.7 for chat-exclusive

rows.measure: Similarity of exclusive latents to other latents relative to the similarity of shared latents to other latents
rows.baseline: Shared latents' maximum similarity to another latent
rows.value: The authors state that base- and chat-exclusive latents are more similar to other latents than shared latents, and call them less exclusive.
rows.note: The text gives the qualitative comparison; numerical values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: This is a crosscoder-architecture result (Figure 11). It is a motivating comparison for the authors' method and gives no numbers in the text. It does not bear on any version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
